newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada union makes first inroads at Starbucks.
newsitem.headline: Canada union makes first inroads at Starbucks.

text.p: The Canadian Auto Workers union declared victory on Friday by securing the first union contract ever at trendy coffee retailer Starbucks Corp. after a tentative deal was struck for 110 workers in Vancouver.
"This is a breakthrough -- the first collective agreement negotiated with Starbucks anywhere in the world," said the union President Buzz Hargrove.
Employees at eight Starbucks coffee bars and a distribution center in Vancouver are the first in the 1,110-store chain to be represented by a union.
Buoyed by the Vancouver deal, the union hopes workers at other Starbucks locations in Canada will join its fold.
A tentative deal for a two-year contract was struck on Thursday after months of negotiations and three days of mediation.
Details of the agreement were not released pending final approval by union members and Seattle-based Starbucks, but ratification appeared certain.
"Both parties are unanimously recommending to their principals acceptance of the package," British Columbia Labor Relations Board mediator Brian Foley said.
For unions the contract raised hopes of making inroads into the fast-growing retail and service sector, an area where organized labor has historically faced an uphill battle.
Union membership in North America, which has traditionally been strongest in manufacturing, has slumped in recent years and unions have seen their influence weakened.
Starbucks officials were unavailable for comment.
Throughout the negotiations, Starbucks maintained that its pay and benefits were superior.
In a brief statement announcing the contract deal, Starbucks noted that the contract covered only eight percent of its employees in British Columbia where it has 94 stores.
The company employs 20,000 workers -- which it calls "partners" -- throughout the United States and Canada.

Hambrecht & Quist analyst Jean-Michel Valette said Starbucks recognized the importance of maintaining good employee relations. Retaining that focus, he said, would be more important to the company's success than whether more outlets were unionized.
Although they became eligible to strike in May, most of the Vancouver workers remained on the job except for those at the bakery distribution center, which is slated to close.
Workers at the distribution center went on strike, which halted deliveries of baked goods to Vancouver-area Starbucks stores for the past two months.
The main issues in the negotiations were wages and work flexibility. The union was demanding a starting wage of C$10 ($7.30) an hour compared to the current C$7 ($5.11).
